Burnham Says You're the Boss. Then He Hands Brussels the Pen.

A red line with an expiry date, a shopping basket that gets dearer, and the trade deals Labour would bin to get back in

By Steve English · 3 November 2026
  • Burnham won a Leave-voting seat by promising not to re-run Brexit, then reached No 10 without a single vote from the country
  • Since then he has said Brexit did "more harm than good" and listed rejoining outright as an option
  • His "red lines" on the Customs Union hold only "for the duration of this Parliament"
  • Inside the EU's Customs Union, tinned beans from outside the bloc face a 17.6% duty and cheap southern-hemisphere apples face entry-price penalties
  • A customs union would hand control of Britain's tariffs to Brussels, wrecking the India deal and Britain's place in the Trans-Pacific Partnership
  • The back door is already open: a food deal that makes Britain copy EU law, with the European Court as final judge
PURPOSE: To set out, in Andy Burnham's own words and from official tariff data, where the Prime Minister is taking Britain's relationship with the EU, and what it will cost.

In June, Andy Burnham stood in Makerfield, a seat that voted an estimated 65% to Leave. He told those voters he would not re-run the Brexit arguments. They elected him. Four days later Keir Starmer resigned, and within a month Burnham was Prime Minister. No general election, no leadership contest, not a single vote cast by the country.

Then the promise started to slide.

Days before Labour conference, he was asked whether he would rule out a pledge to rejoin the EU in Labour's next manifesto. That question, he said, was "for another day".

The other day came quickly. At conference he told the country Brexit had done "more harm than good". Asked by the BBC whether he wanted Britain back in, he ran through the menu: a customs union, the single market, "or we could go all the way."

Then he went to the Commons, called overturning Brexit "an option", and declared it would be a "major dereliction of duty" not to pursue a new deal with Brussels. He told MPs the British public would be "the boss" at every stage. Around the same time, he went on a podcast and claimed Russia interfered in the 2016 referendum, while producing no evidence and no source.

By late October he was on breakfast television insisting he was still "respecting" what he told Makerfield.

Last weekend he wanted an "honest discussion" about bringing back EU freedom of movement. Today he says he never proposed it.

That is the pattern. Promise one thing to the voters who elect you. Say the opposite to the party that crowns you. Deny it when you're caught.

The red line with a sell-by date

Burnham insists he will keep Labour's manifesto red lines: no customs union, no single market, no free movement. Read the small print. Those red lines hold "for the duration of this Parliament". He has already signalled he could fight the next election on taking Britain back in.

His own MPs are not hiding where they want to go. Andrew Lewin, founder of the campaign group Remain Labour, wants talks on the single market and customs union opened now, then put to the country "in a couple of years". Thirteen Labour MPs have already voted to negotiate a UK–EU customs union. The Liberal Democrats want both. And the Prime Minister has written to his own Cabinet telling ministers not to say publicly which option they back, while his Home Secretary insists the manifesto must stand.

When Facts4EU published its costings, the Government's reply was that "there has been no proposal to rejoin the Customs Union." The Prime Minister himself put it on the table at conference.

Your shopping basket, Brussels prices

A customs union means one thing above all: Britain charges the EU's tariffs on goods from the rest of the world. The EU sets those tariffs to protect EU producers, not British shoppers.

Take tinned beans. The EU charges 17.6% on shelled beans, prepared or preserved, imported from outside the bloc. That is the protection wall around Europe's canneries, and Britain would be back behind it.

Take apples. Britain charges nothing on most imported fresh apples. The EU charges seasonal duty of up to 8% on top of an "entry price" system: the cheaper the apples, the bigger the penalty. That system exists to stop cheap Australian and New Zealand fruit undercutting European growers. Those are the very apples that keep British supermarket prices down out of season.

Take sugar. Facts4EU calculates that EU duties on raw cane sugar would work out at an effective import tax of 56–72%, against zero under Britain's own quota.

This is the "pragmatic" option Labour wants to discuss during a cost-of-living crisis.

The deals they would bin

Britain's trade deal with India came into force on 15 July this year. Britain joined the Trans-Pacific Partnership on 1 September. UK exports to the Trans-Pacific bloc reached £86.3 billion in the year to March 2026, up 8.1% on the year before.

None of that survives a customs union. Inside one, Britain cannot set its own tariffs, and without its own tariffs it has nothing to offer in a trade negotiation. Brussels sets the terms, and Britain follows. Every deal signed since 2020 would be up for renegotiation, or gone.

The back door is already open

While the customs union "conversation" grabs the headlines, the real handover is already on the table for the 20 November summit in Brussels.

The Government's answer to the Facts4EU report was its agri-food deal, which it says will end costly paperwork. Read what that deal is. Under the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, Britain's food and farming rules must match EU rules, and whenever Brussels changes its rules, Britain must change too. Britain pays a financial contribution. Disputes go to a panel that ensures the European Court of Justice is "the ultimate authority" on EU law.

To deliver it, the Government plans a European Partnership Bill. Parliament's own library notes press reports that the bill will include Henry VIII powers: ministers changing Acts of Parliament by order.

So the public is "the boss". Parliament gets a rubber stamp. Brussels gets the pen. And the Prime Minister keeps telling you nothing has been proposed.

On 20 November we find out how much has already been given away.
